headline: Arkaz, TotalEnergies, Hamte Group and Mectco take first stands as Big 5 Construct Saudi opens
deck: The first-timer list says who now thinks the Saudi construction supply chain is worth a stand, and the licence numbers behind the ministry's patronage say why.
excerpt: Big 5 Construct Saudi 2026 opened at Riyadh Front under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources with more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries. Among them are companies exhibiting at the show for the first time, from Arkaz five months after its acquisition by Master Builders Solutions to TotalEnergies, Hamte Group, Mectco, Lanmix and K-Flex Insulation.
content:
Big 5 Construct Saudi 2026 opened in Riyadh on Sunday under the patronage of the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources, bringing more than 1,000 exhibitors from over 50 countries to the Riyadh Front Exhibition and Conference Center for four days, with the organiser expecting more than 35,000 trade visitors before the show closes on 2 September. The opening itself is reported in BrentDesk's account of the ceremony. This report is about who is new on the floor, and what a first stand says about the market.

The organiser lists Arkaz, TotalEnergies, Hamte Group and Mectco among the first-time exhibitors at this edition, according to its line-up. Arkaz, the construction chemicals producer with plants in Dammam and Jeddah, arrives at its first Big 5 Construct Saudi some five months after Master Builders Solutions completed its acquisition of the business, a debut covered in BrentDesk's report on the stand. TotalEnergies is on the same list. Hamte Group shows construction technologies and engineering solutions, and Mectco waste management and environmental products. International first-timers include Australia's Lanmix, with steel fibre reinforcement, and Egypt's K-Flex Insulation, presenting thermal, acoustic and fire-stopping systems.

The larger names on the floor are familiar: CPC Holding, the fire protection group NAFFCO and Al Yamamah Steel Industries, alongside Masa, Gibus and Al Muqarram. The organiser has highlighted Masdar's Kronospan carbon-negative wood-based panels and engineered boards, Galaxy Technology's Albion Valves with carbon transparency across its cast-iron range, Star Factory's spray polyurethane foam roofing and waterproofing, Keller's ground improvement and foundation work, and Al-Futtaim Engineering's integrated facilities and energy management.

A first stand at Riyadh Front is a decision about the market rather than about the show. Exhibiting is cheap against the cost of a Saudi entity, a warehouse and a service engineer, which is what buyers here now expect to find behind a stand, so a company that takes one for the first time is usually announcing the larger commitment rather than testing the water. The change in what international companies ask, from how to sell into Saudi Arabia to how to be present in it, is the subject of a separate BrentDesk piece.

Ministry patronage is not decoration. The Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources sits at the centre of the Kingdom's industrial licensing and localisation machinery, and the sector it oversees has been expanding quickly: 13,660 industrial facilities were active at the end of April 2026, up more than 11 per cent year on year, with 322 new industrial licences issued in April carrying investment above SAR 12.33 billion. A construction supply-chain exhibition held under that patronage is, in part, a shop window for domestic manufacturing capacity, and the first-timer list is partly a list of companies that want to be counted in it.

The demand backdrop is steady rather than uniform. Saudi construction output is forecast to grow 6.2 per cent in 2026 to about SAR 232.14 billion. Contract awards tracked by the Saudi Contractors Authority reached their 2026 high in May at more than SR 30.03 billion across 18 projects, with infrastructure accounting for 10 projects worth over SR 25 billion, and June brought the year's highest project count, 25 awards worth more than SR 29.5 billion, with building and construction taking 14 of them and 56 per cent of the value. The National Housing Company led project owners by value in June, ahead of Saudi Aramco.

Against that, several giga-project programmes have been re-phased or re-scoped over the past year, and cost pressure has become a standing item in contractor conversations. The practical consequence for the exhibition floor is that buyers arrive with sharper questions about lifecycle cost, lead times, local stock and after-sales support rather than headline price alone, and the newcomers will be asked them first.

Big 5 Construct Saudi runs daily at Riyadh Front until 2 September, with a conference programme across nine topic areas alongside the halls.
